claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a favorable strength–ductility combination.
A controlled amount of grain-boundary-pinning particles will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
The intervention is the introduction of grain-boundary-pinning particles.
The applicable thermal exposure is 800 °C for 100 hours.
Thermal exposure is followed by tensile loading at room temperature.
The introduced particles will inhibit grain growth during thermal exposure.
The introduced particles will reduce the formation of detrimental precipitates during thermal exposure.
Inhibiting grain growth and reducing detrimental precipitates will preserve toughness.
After identical exposure and loading, the particle-containing alloy will have higher toughness than the alloy without particles.
The relevant boundary conditions include exposure temperature and duration and loading rate and magnitude.
The optimal particle amount and type and the effects of particle distribution and morphology are uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing otherwise identical particle-containing and particle-free alloys after thermal exposure and loading.
Toughness can be evaluated using a measure such as Charpy impact energy, alongside grain-size and precipitate characterization.
Equivalent or lower toughness in the particle-containing alloy relative to the particle-free control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated loading regime is tensile loading, whereas the example toughness measurement is Charpy impact energy, which uses impact loading. The experiment does not clarify whether Charpy testing replaces the tensile-loading step or follows it.
